subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Explain solids, liquids and gases with the particle model
A temperature change is the same in kelvin and in degrees Celsius
Kelvin temperature measures average particle kinetic energy
Internal energy: random kinetic plus intermolecular potential energy
Temperature difference decides which way energy flows
Phase changes happen at constant temperature
Calculate energy transfers with specific heat capacity and latent heat
The three mechanisms of thermal energy transfer
Conduction as particles sharing kinetic energy
Radiation from a black body: the Stefan–Boltzmann law
Link apparent brightness, luminosity and distance

questions.q: A pure substance is heated steadily from a solid until it has completely boiled. According to the molecular model, which statement about its molecules is correct?
options: Their mean separation increases greatly on melting and increases again on boiling.
Their mean separation changes little on melting but increases greatly on boiling.
The molecules themselves get larger on melting, and larger again on boiling.
The molecules start to move only on melting, and they move faster still on boiling.
optionWhy: A student who pictures liquid molecules as widely spaced picks this. Liquids are almost incompressible and have densities close to their solids, so the separation hardly changes on melting; the large increase happens on boiling.

In a solid and a liquid the molecules are close together, which is why their densities are similar; melting frees them from fixed positions without separating them much. On boiling they move far apart: the gas is roughly a thousand times less dense than the liquid.

A student who gives particles the properties of the bulk material picks this. The molecules stay the same size throughout; what changes is how far apart they are, how they are arranged and how they move.

A student who thinks solid particles are motionless picks this. Molecules in a solid already vibrate about fixed positions; melting lets them slide past one another. And during boiling itself the temperature, and so the average kinetic energy, is constant.
questions.explain: In a solid and a liquid the molecules are close together, which is why their densities are similar; melting frees them from fixed positions without separating them much. On boiling they move far apart: the gas is roughly a thousand times less dense than the liquid.

questions.q: The density of aluminium is 2.7 g cm⁻³. What is the volume, in m³, of an aluminium block of mass 0.081 kg?
optionWhy: A student who finds 30 cm³ correctly and then divides by 100 to convert to m³ gets 0.30 m³, a block the size of a large cupboard. A cubic metre is (100 cm)³ = 10⁶ cm³, so 30 cm³ = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ m³.

A student who divides the mass in kilograms by the density in grams per cubic centimetre gets 0.081/2.7 = 0.030 and calls it m³. The units must match: use 81 g with 2.7 g cm⁻³, or 0.081 kg with 2700 kg m⁻³.
ρ = m/V, so V = m/ρ = 81 g/2.7 g cm⁻³ = 30 cm³. Since 1 cm³ = (10⁻² m)³ = 10⁻⁶ m³, V = 30 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ m³. (In SI: V = 0.081 kg/2700 kg m⁻³ gives the same result.)
A student who treats density as volume divided by mass multiplies instead of dividing: 81 × 2.7 = 219 cm³ = 2.2 × 10⁻⁴ m³. Density is mass per unit volume, so V = m/ρ.
questions.explain: ρ = m/V, so V = m/ρ = 81 g/2.7 g cm⁻³ = 30 cm³. Since 1 cm³ = (10⁻² m)³ = 10⁻⁶ m³, V = 30 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ m³. (In SI: V = 0.081 kg/2700 kg m⁻³ gives the same result.)
questions.working: ρ = m/V ⇒ V = m/ρ. In SI: ρ = 2.7 g cm⁻³ = 2.7 × 10³ kg m⁻³; V = 0.081 kg/(2.7 × 10³ kg m⁻³) = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ m³ (= 30 cm³).

questions.q: Which statement about the Kelvin and Celsius temperature scales is correct?
options: A Kelvin temperature is converted to degrees Celsius by adding 273, since both directions use the same rule.
A temperature has the same numerical value on both scales, as the kelvin is the SI name for the degree Celsius.
A Celsius temperature is converted to kelvin by adding 273, whether the Celsius value is above or below zero.
A temperature below the freezing point of water is negative on the Kelvin scale, exactly as it is on the Celsius scale.
optionWhy: A student who remembers '273' but not which way it goes picks this. Kelvin values are the larger numbers (0 °C is 273 K), so going from kelvin to Celsius means subtracting 273: 112 K is −161 °C, not 385 °C.

A student who treats the kelvin as a renamed degree picks this. The kelvin and the degree Celsius are the same size, but the scales start in different places: 0 K is −273 °C, so a given temperature has different values on the two scales.
T/K = t/°C + 273 for every temperature. The two scales have divisions of the same size and differ only in their zero, which is 273 °C lower on the Kelvin scale, so −78 °C is 195 K and 27 °C is 300 K.

A student who thinks of the Kelvin scale as a relabelled Celsius scale picks this. 0 K is the lowest possible temperature, so Kelvin temperatures are never negative: water freezes at 273 K, and −78 °C is +195 K.
questions.explain: T/K = t/°C + 273 for every temperature. The two scales have divisions of the same size and differ only in their zero, which is 273 °C lower on the Kelvin scale, so −78 °C is 195 K and 27 °C is 300 K.
questions.working: T/K = t/°C + 273 for every temperature, e.g. −78 °C → −78 + 273 = 195 K and 27 °C → 300 K; the reverse conversion subtracts 273 (112 K → −161 °C).

questions.q: Sample P is warmed from 10 °C to 30 °C. Sample Q is warmed from 290 K to 310 K. Which statement about the two temperature changes is correct?
options: P's rise of 20 °C is equivalent to a rise of 293 K.
The changes differ, since kelvins and °C differ in size.
Both undergo the same temperature change, 20 K.
P's rise is larger, since P's temperature tripled.
optionWhy: A student who adds 273 to every Celsius value picks this. The 273 cancels in a difference: (30 + 273) − (10 + 273) = 20 K. Only a temperature, never a change, has 273 added.

A student who assumes the two scales have different-sized degrees, as the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales do, picks this. The kelvin was defined to be the same size as the degree Celsius, so a change of 20 °C is a change of 20 K, the same as Q's.
P: ΔT = 30 − 10 = 20 °C, which is 20 K because the kelvin and the degree Celsius are the same size. Q: ΔT = 310 − 290 = 20 K. The changes are equal.
A student who treats a ratio of Celsius temperatures as meaningful picks this. On the absolute scale P goes from 283 K to 303 K, a factor of only 1.07; the change, 20 K, is the same as Q's.
questions.explain: P: ΔT = 30 − 10 = 20 °C, which is 20 K because the kelvin and the degree Celsius are the same size. Q: ΔT = 310 − 290 = 20 K. The changes are equal.
questions.working: P: ΔT = 30 °C − 10 °C = 20 °C = 20 K. Q: ΔT = 310 K − 290 K = 20 K. Equal changes. (P in kelvin: 283 K to 303 K, ratio 1.07, not 3.)

questions.q: The average kinetic energy of the molecules of a gas is 8.28 × 10⁻²¹ J. Take k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. What is the temperature of the gas in degrees Celsius?
optionWhy: A student who finds T = 400 K correctly but thinks kelvin and Celsius values are the same stops here. 400 K is 400 − 273 = 127 °C.
A student who finds 400 K and then adds 273 gets 673. Adding 273 converts Celsius to kelvin; converting kelvin to Celsius needs 273 subtracted.
A student who takes E̅_k = k_B T gets T = 8.28 × 10⁻²¹/1.38 × 10⁻²³ = 600 K = 327 °C. The relationship is E̅_k = (3/2)k_B T, so T is two-thirds of that, 400 K.

questions.q: Which of the following is the internal energy of a system?
options: The total random kinetic energy of its molecules plus their total intermolecular potential energy
The total random kinetic energy of its molecules, which is the quantity its temperature measures
The kinetic energy of the body's motion plus its gravitational potential energy and its molecules' energy
The quantity of heat that is stored in the system, which it gives out again when it cools down
optionWhy: This is the guide's definition: the potential energy arising from the forces between molecules plus the kinetic energy of their random motion.

A student who leaves out the potential-energy part picks this. Internal energy also includes the intermolecular potential energy, which is what changes during melting and boiling. (Temperature measures the AVERAGE kinetic energy, not the total.)

A student who reads 'internal' as 'all the energy the body has' picks this. The kinetic energy of the body as a whole and its gravitational potential energy are macroscopic stores, not part of internal energy.

A student who thinks of heat as a substance held in a body picks this. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; what a body contains is internal energy, defined in terms of molecular kinetic and potential energy.
questions.explain: This is the guide's definition: the potential energy arising from the forces between molecules plus the kinetic energy of their random motion.

questions.q: A 0.20 kg copper block at 80 °C is lowered into a large tank containing 200 kg of water at 20 °C. The water has far more internal energy than the block. Which statement describes the resultant thermal energy transfer?
options: From the block to the water, until they reach the same temperature.
From the water to the block, since the water has more internal energy.
Coldness passes from the water into the block, so the block cools down.
From the block to the water, until they have equal internal energies.
optionWhy: The direction of the resultant transfer is set by temperature difference alone: from the hotter block to the cooler water. It stops at thermal equilibrium, when the temperatures are equal, just above 20 °C here because the tank is so large.

A student who treats internal energy as if it were temperature picks this. The water's large internal energy comes from its large mass; each water molecule has less average kinetic energy than each copper particle, and energy flows from high to low temperature.
A student who thinks of cold as something that flows picks this. Only energy is transferred: the block cools because it loses energy to the water, and nothing called 'cold' enters it.

A student who thinks energy levels out like water between tanks picks this. The direction is right, but transfer stops when the TEMPERATURES are equal; the 200 kg of water still has vastly more internal energy than the block.
questions.explain: The direction of the resultant transfer is set by temperature difference alone: from the hotter block to the cooler water. It stops at thermal equilibrium, when the temperatures are equal, just above 20 °C here because the tank is so large.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes evaporation from boiling for water at atmospheric pressure?
options: Evaporation occurs only at the boiling point, and only at the surface; boiling occurs throughout the whole liquid.
Evaporation occurs only at the surface and at any temperature; boiling occurs throughout, at the boiling point.
Boiling produces bubbles of air or of hydrogen and oxygen; evaporation produces water vapour.
Boiling occurs throughout while the temperature keeps rising; evaporation occurs at the surface.
optionWhy: A student who links all vapour formation to the boiling point picks this. Puddles and washing dry at everyday temperatures: evaporation happens at any temperature, at the surface.

Surface molecules with enough kinetic energy escape at any temperature, which is evaporation. Boiling happens once the liquid reaches its boiling point (100 °C at atmospheric pressure), with vapour forming in bubbles throughout the liquid.
A student who thinks the bubbles in boiling water are air or its elements picks this. Boiling is a phase change: the bubbles are water vapour formed inside the liquid.

A student who expects continued heating always to raise the temperature picks this. While water boils at constant pressure its temperature stays at the boiling point; the energy supplied is latent heat.
questions.explain: Surface molecules with enough kinetic energy escape at any temperature, which is evaporation. Boiling happens once the liquid reaches its boiling point (100 °C at atmospheric pressure), with vapour forming in bubbles throughout the liquid.

questions.q: An electric kettle heats 250 g of water from 18 °C to 90 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. How much energy is transferred to the water? Ignore energy transferred to the kettle and surroundings.
optionWhy: Convert the mass first: m = 250 g = 0.250 kg. Q = mcΔT = 0.250 × 4.18 × 10³ × (90 − 18) = 0.250 × 4180 × 72 = 7.5 × 10⁴ J. A temperature change of 72 °C is 72 K.
A student who adds 273 to the temperature change uses ΔT = 345 K and gets 0.250 × 4180 × 345 = 3.6 × 10⁵ J. A change of 72 °C is a change of 72 K; the 273 cancels in the subtraction.
A student who substitutes the mass in grams, as given, uses m = 250 and gets 250 × 4180 × 72 = 7.5 × 10⁷ J. Specific heat capacity is per kilogram, so convert first.
A student who uses the final temperature, 90 °C, in place of the change gets 0.250 × 4180 × 90 = 9.4 × 10⁴ J. ΔT is the change, 90 − 18 = 72 K.
questions.explain: Convert the mass first: m = 250 g = 0.250 kg. Q = mcΔT = 0.250 × 4.18 × 10³ × (90 − 18) = 0.250 × 4180 × 72 = 7.5 × 10⁴ J. A temperature change of 72 °C is 72 K.

questions.q: 0.40 kg of ice at 0 °C is melted and the water is then warmed to 20 °C. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; specific latent heat of vaporization of water = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹; specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the total energy that must be supplied?
optionWhy: A student who thinks melting at constant temperature needs no energy calculates only the warming, 0.40 × 4180 × 20 = 3.3 × 10⁴ J. Melting absorbs latent heat, here 1.3 × 10⁵ J, four times the energy needed for the warming.
A student who uses the latent heat of vaporization for the melting gets 0.40 × 2.26 × 10⁶ + 3.34 × 10⁴ = 9.4 × 10⁵ J. Melting is fusion; L_v applies to boiling, which does not happen here.
A student who adds 273 to the temperature change uses ΔT = 293 K for the warming and gets 1.336 × 10⁵ + 0.40 × 4180 × 293 = 6.2 × 10⁵ J. The rise from 0 °C to 20 °C is 20 K.

questions.q: Which statement about the mechanisms of thermal energy transfer is correct?
options: All three are directed upwards, because heat naturally rises from warm places.
Convection can occur in solids as well as in liquids and gases, just like conduction.
Thermal radiation is emitted only by very hot objects, such as the Sun or a fire.
Only thermal radiation can cross a vacuum; conduction and convection both need a medium.
optionWhy: A student who thinks heat itself rises picks this. It is hot FLUID that rises in convection; conduction and radiation carry energy in any direction, including downwards.
A student who treats convection as any 'carrying of heat' picks this. Convection needs bulk movement of the material, which only fluids can undergo; in solids energy is transferred by conduction.
A student who knows only glowing sources radiate noticeably picks this. Every body above absolute zero emits thermal radiation; cool bodies emit less power and mainly in the infrared.

Conduction passes energy between particles and convection moves the fluid itself, so both need matter. Thermal radiation is electromagnetic waves, which cross empty space; this is how energy reaches the Earth from the Sun.
questions.explain: Conduction passes energy between particles and convection moves the fluid itself, so both need matter. Thermal radiation is electromagnetic waves, which cross empty space; this is how energy reaches the Earth from the Sun.

questions.q: One end of a glass rod is held in a flame. How does the molecular model explain conduction of energy along the rod?
options: Hot particles travel along the rod from the hot end to the cold end, carrying their energy with them.
Faster-vibrating particles at the hot end pass kinetic energy to their slower neighbours, and so on along the rod.
Heat flows along the rod like a fluid, filling the spaces between the particles as it goes.
Particles at the hot end expand and push against their neighbours, passing the heat along.
optionWhy: A student who merges conduction with convection picks this. In a solid the particles only vibrate about fixed positions; energy is passed from particle to particle, but the particles do not travel.

Particles at the hot end have a greater average kinetic energy. Through collisions and the forces between neighbours they pass energy to particles with less, and the energy spreads towards the cold end while the particles stay in place.
A student who thinks of heat as a substance picks this. Nothing material flows: energy is passed on through the interactions of particles with different kinetic energies.
A student who thinks particles swell when heated picks this. Particles do not change size; those at the hot end vibrate with more kinetic energy and pass energy on to their neighbours.
questions.explain: Particles at the hot end have a greater average kinetic energy. Through collisions and the forces between neighbours they pass energy to particles with less, and the energy spreads towards the cold end while the particles stay in place.

questions.q: The rate of thermal energy transfer by conduction is given by ΔQ/Δt = −kA(ΔT/Δx). What does the minus sign show?
options: The rate of energy transfer falls steadily with time and along the length of the conductor.
Cold is conducted in the opposite direction to heat, from the cold end to the hot end.
Energy flows towards lower temperature: where T falls along +x, the net flow is along +x.
The conductor is losing energy, so ΔQ/Δt is a negative quantity for every conducting material.
optionWhy: A student who reads every minus sign as 'decreasing' picks this. In steady state the rate is constant in time and the same through every cross-section; the sign shows the direction of flow.
A student who thinks cold is something that flows picks this. Only energy is transferred, and it flows from higher to lower temperature; nothing flows the other way.
Where the temperature decreases along +x, ΔT/Δx is negative, so −kA(ΔT/Δx) is positive: energy flows in the +x direction, from hot to cold. The minus sign encodes the direction of flow.

A student who links minus signs with losses picks this. In steady state a conductor gains energy at its hot face as fast as it loses it at its cold face, and ΔQ/Δt is positive in the direction of decreasing temperature.
questions.explain: Where the temperature decreases along +x, ΔT/Δx is negative, so −kA(ΔT/Δx) is positive: energy flows in the +x direction, from hot to cold. The minus sign encodes the direction of flow.

questions.q: Warm air rises above a radiator in a cold room. Which is the correct explanation?
options: Heat naturally rises, so the thermal energy from the radiator moves upwards and carries the air along with it.
Each air molecule expands when it is heated, so it becomes lighter than a cold molecule and floats upwards.
Warm air has almost no weight, unlike the colder air around it, so nothing holds it down and it simply floats upwards.
Air heated by the radiator expands, so it is less dense than the cooler air around it, which sinks and pushes it up.
optionWhy: A student who thinks heat itself rises picks this. It is the warm air that rises, because it is less dense than its surroundings; the energy is carried by the air, not the other way round.
A student who thinks molecules swell when heated picks this. Molecules keep their size and mass; the air expands because its molecules move further apart, which lowers the density of the air.
A student who thinks hot gases are weightless picks this. Warm air has weight; it rises because a given volume of it weighs less than the same volume of the cooler air around it.
Warmed air expands, so a given volume has less mass: its density falls. The denser, cooler air around it sinks beneath it and pushes it upwards, and a convection current forms.
questions.explain: Warmed air expands, so a given volume has less mass: its density falls. The denser, cooler air around it sinks beneath it and pushes it upwards, and a convection current forms.

questions.q: A small metal sphere of radius 5.0 cm is heated to 527 °C. Treat it as a black body and take σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. What power does the sphere emit as thermal radiation?
optionWhy: A student who uses the Celsius temperature, 527, in T⁴ gets 1.4 × 10² W. The Stefan–Boltzmann law needs the absolute temperature, 800 K; with a fourth power the error is large.
A student who uses πr², the area of the disc the sphere appears as, gets a quarter of the true value, 1.8 × 10² W. Radiation leaves the whole surface, area 4πr².
A student who substitutes r = 5.0 (centimetres) gets an area 10⁴ times too large and 7.3 × 10⁶ W. Convert to r = 0.050 m before using σ in W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

questions.q: Two stars appear equally bright when viewed from the Earth. Which statement must be true?
options: Equal power per unit area reaches Earth from each.
Each star radiates the same total power out into space.
The two stars are at the same distance from the Earth.
The two stars must have equal surface temperatures.
optionWhy: Apparent brightness is the power received per unit area at the observer. Equal apparent brightness means exactly this, and nothing more about the stars themselves.
A student who equates brightness with luminosity picks this. Equal brightness can arise from a luminous distant star and a dim nearby one; b = L/4πd² depends on both L and d.
A student who thinks brightness depends only on distance picks this. Stars differ enormously in luminosity, so equally bright stars can be at very different distances.
A student who thinks brightness is set by temperature alone picks this. Brightness depends on luminosity, which depends on surface area as well as temperature, and on distance.
questions.explain: Apparent brightness is the power received per unit area at the observer. Equal apparent brightness means exactly this, and nothing more about the stars themselves.

questions.q: A star has a luminosity of 40 L⊙ and is 25 ly from the Earth. Take L⊙ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W and 1 ly = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m. What is the apparent brightness of the star at the Earth?
options: 2.0 × 10²⁴ W m⁻²
optionWhy: A student who divides by πd² instead of 4πd² gets a value four times too large, 8.7 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻². The power spreads over the whole sphere of radius d, area 4πd².
A student who uses b = L/d² gets 2.7 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻², about 12.6 times too large. The area over which the power spreads is 4πd².
A student who substitutes d = 25 (light-years) gets 2.0 × 10²⁴ W m⁻². The distance must be in metres: 25 ly = 2.37 × 10¹⁷ m.

questions.q: A surface at 27 °C can be modelled as a black body. Wien's displacement law: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K. At what wavelength is its emission most intense?
options: 1.1 × 10⁻⁴ m, in the far infrared
8.7 × 10⁻¹ m, in the radio band
3.6 × 10⁻¹³ m, in the gamma-ray band
9.7 × 10⁻⁶ m, in the infrared
optionWhy: A student who uses the Celsius temperature gets 2.9 × 10⁻³/27 = 1.1 × 10⁻⁴ m. Wien's law needs the absolute temperature, 300 K.
A student who thinks λ_max increases with temperature multiplies instead of dividing: 2.9 × 10⁻³ × 300 = 0.87 m. λ_max is inversely proportional to T.
A student who mixes Wien's law with the Stefan–Boltzmann law divides by T⁴ and gets 3.6 × 10⁻¹³ m. Wien's law uses T to the first power: λ_max = 2.9 × 10⁻³/T.
T = 27 + 273 = 300 K; λ_max = 2.9 × 10⁻³/300 = 9.7 × 10⁻⁶ m (about 10 μm), in the infrared. Everyday objects emit mainly infrared, which is why they do not glow visibly.
questions.explain: T = 27 + 273 = 300 K; λ_max = 2.9 × 10⁻³/300 = 9.7 × 10⁻⁶ m (about 10 μm), in the infrared. Everyday objects emit mainly infrared, which is why they do not glow visibly.
questions.working: T = 27 + 273 = 300 K. λ_max = (2.9 × 10⁻³ m K)/(300 K) = 9.7 × 10⁻⁶ m, which is in the infrared (about 10 μm).

questions.q: A black body is heated to a higher temperature. How does its emission spectrum change?
options: It emits more at every wavelength, and the peak moves to a longer wavelength.
It emits more at every wavelength, and its peak moves to a shorter wavelength.
Its peak moves to shorter wavelengths, so it emits less at long wavelengths.
It emits only one wavelength, λ_max, which gets shorter as it gets hotter.
optionWhy: A student who links higher temperature with longer (redder) wavelengths picks this. λ_max is inversely proportional to T: the peak moves to shorter wavelengths as T rises.
A hotter black body emits more intensely at every wavelength, so the whole curve rises, and by Wien's law λ_max = 2.9 × 10⁻³/T the peak moves to a shorter wavelength.
A student who pictures the curve sliding sideways picks this. The hotter curve lies above the cooler one at every wavelength, including long ones; it rises as the peak shifts.
A student who thinks a black body emits only its peak wavelength picks this. The spectrum is continuous over all wavelengths; λ_max is only where the intensity is greatest.
questions.explain: A hotter black body emits more intensely at every wavelength, so the whole curve rises, and by Wien's law λ_max = 2.9 × 10⁻³/T the peak moves to a shorter wavelength.
